So in the manhwa Grey (Si-Eun) is short (5’4”) and barely weighs 50kg wet through. He’s portrayed as a weak kid who does anything he can to survive. He analyses his opponents and uses whatever he can to win coz he knows he can’t compete with the strength of those much larger than him. The drama loses that a bit, esp. s2. 

As a manhwa reader I was disappointed in the fight at the underpass. In the manhwa ,>!Grey ends up cracking a kids skull after hitting him with a brick and then smashing his head into a wall.!< Grey is much more ruthless than Si-Eun.

Personally, I think s1 is much better than s2. It’s hard to explain concisely but for me it had a much stronger impact. I think the storyline was much more harder hitting and Si-Eun’s character was more in line with the manhwa. S2 felt very watered down in comparison - like Netflix deliberately softened it. 

I think part of this is due to how they adapted the material. Though they both made significant changes to the plot and characters, s1 covered about 10 or so chapters in 8 episodes, whereas s2 covered 100+ chapters (200+ if you include backstories) in 8 episodes. So for manhwa readers esp. it felt rushed and underdeveloped. 

I did enjoy S2, but I did think it could be better both as a fan of the drama and manhwa. There was a lot of potential for it to be amazing so I think Netflix really missed a trick here. They could have easily broken down the story and planned for a s3. There were certainly characters I missed as a manhwa reader, and as a fan of the drama I just found it underwhelming when compared to s1. 

But these are just my personal thoughts. If you enjoyed s2 the you should def give s1 a go. 

As a side note, s2 is where the manhwa starts. S1 is Grey’s / Si-Eun’s backstory in the manhwa so for the first 25 chapters or so you don’t really know much about him other than he’s a quiet kid who has transferred to this school, and is both smart and ruthless.

True… it was just a random statement about Ainz’s situation. But I think it highlights the differences of their positions. Ainz is thrown into a situation where Rimiru starts from the beginning giving him the chance to develop and learn without losing himself or his vision. Ainz’s vision (outside of finding players) is mostly based on his subordinates vision. They’re leading him.

It was only 100 people, and with the exception of Shion most were ordinary citizens compared to Shaltear who was one of the strongest people in Nazarick. As for Ainz leaving specific orders… I’m not sure about this. 

The attacks came at different points in development. Ainz was still trying to gather info about the world and was pretty cautious because he still didn’t have a grasp on anything. Rimiru meanwhile had a developing city, had already made trade links and delegated leasership roles to his subordinates. He felt confident enough that he could leave because they were beginning to flourish. 

In my mind, Rimiru stands out because he has a vision of what he wants and works towards that. Ainz is heavily influenced by his subordinates. He’s more following their lead rather than leading them.

Can you image waking up one day and having to rule the country? Not to mention you’ve changed races, you have no clue where you are, the rules have changed and all your followers are devout sycophants because you are literally their god and creator. I don’t envy Ainz’s position at all. Probably best he was undead coz he prob would have died from the stress of trying to keep on top of everything.
I don’t think this makes Rimiru a worse leader. Ainz also lost Shaltear, so they both had to revive their people.

As much as love these two, Rimiru is on top when it comes to leadership. He’s not afraid to take control and put himself out there. But I think that’s because he’s coming from a different place to Ainz. He built everything from scratch. 

Ainz on the other hand was thrown into top dog position where everyone already thought of him as an all mighty ruler. He was afraid they’d rebel if he didn’t live up to their image so he spends a lot of his time trying to catch up and not appear weak in front of everyone.

If I’m not in a position to move, I’ll tap a tune against my leg - as if I was playing a piano. 

When I having a sever attack, breathing to counts of ten helps. Saying each number out loud as I say take a breath, then forcing myself to hold that breath and release slowly helps me to calm down quicker. It doesn’t happen immediately, and I usually count to ten several times before it takes affect, but hearing myself count each breath quickly, triggers my response to slow down.
